title: Prosecutor v. Pavle Strugar — shelling of Dubrovnik's Old Town
question: Is the commander criminally responsible for the JNA shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on 6 December 1991?
facts: Hostilities between the JNA and Croatian forces began in the south coastal area of Croatia in September 1991, and a blockade of Dubrovnik began on 1 October 1991. JNA forces under the accused's command conducted operations toward Dubrovnik from 23 to 26 October and from 9 to 13 November; the wider city and the Old Town were shelled during those periods. On 5 December 1991, Croatian and JNA representatives met in Cavtat for negotiations concerning the blockade, with discussions planned to continue the next day. At about 0550 on 6 December, JNA artillery began firing, initially mainly toward the elevated position above the Old Town. Two JNA infantry units, each with tank support and comprising fewer than 40 soldiers in total, attempted to capture that position, which was defended by Croatian forces. Croatian mortar and machine-gun fire against the attacking troops came from the wider city, but not from the Old Town. JNA artillery also fired at Croatian firing positions in the wider city. Shelling of residential areas, including the Old Town and its port, began early in the attack; firing later shifted toward the wider city, including the Old Town, and continued for over ten and a half hours. The shelling killed two civilians, seriously wounded two people, damaged 52 buildings and structures in the Old Town, and destroyed six of them. The Old Town had a resident population of between 7,000 and 8,000 and had been entered on the World Heritage List in 1979. The accused commanded the Second Operational Group; Admiral Jokić commanded the 9 VPS, which was under the operational command of the accused's group. On 6 December, Minister Rudolf, the European Community Monitoring Mission and Dubrovnik's civil authorities made repeated protests about the JNA artillery attack to JNA representatives, the accused and General Kadijević. After an ECMM protest, General Kadijević telephoned the accused between 0600 and 0700; the accused telephoned Admiral Jokić at about 0700. The accused and Jokić flew to Belgrade that afternoon on Kadijević's order and returned to their commands at about 1730. Jokić conducted an inquiry afterwards. The accused took no investigative or disciplinary action concerning the attack. The accused had ordered an attempt to capture the elevated position and issued a cease-fire order effective at 1115 hours to some JNA artillery units. The attack and shelling continued after that order.
holding: The Trial Chamber's result was split. It found Strugar guilty under Article 7(3) of the Statute on Count 3, attacks on civilians, and Count 6, destruction or wilful damage to institutions dedicated to religion, charity and education, the arts and sciences, historic monuments and works of art and science, as violations of Article 3 of the Statute. It did not find him guilty under Article 7(1) on any of the six counts. The Chamber sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment.
key_reasoning: The Accused had legal and effective control of the JNA forces involved in the military action at Dubrovnik.

From about 0700 on 6 December, the risk that JNA artillery was shelling the Old Town was sufficiently real and serious that the Accused should have determined whether the shelling was occurring and ensured it stopped.
The Accused had authority after the attack to investigate and take disciplinary or other adverse action against the perpetrators, but took no action.
The elements of responsibility under Article 7(3) were established; the Chamber recorded convictions on Counts 3 and 6 under Article 3 of the Statute.
